title: Awake again
hookLine: Muslims wake thanking God who gave life after sleep, a small death (Bukhari)

lines: A SECOND OF SIMPLY BEING HERE.
cards: The alarm goes off. Before the phone, before the news, before the first worry of the day arrives, there's a second or two when you're simply here again. Eyes open, ceiling, light at the edge of the curtain.
Usually that moment slips by unnoticed. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is reported to have filled it with a few words of thanks, and the words are still said on waking.
They treat every waking as a small return from something like death.

teach.b: First, sleep as a small death. The Qur'an draws the comparison itself.

In paraphrase of Surah thirty-nine, verse forty-two: God takes souls at the time of their death, and takes the souls of those who have not died during their sleep; He keeps those for whom He has decreed death, and sends the others back until an appointed time.
In that picture, every night is a letting go, and every morning a sending back.

teach.h: THE FIRST WORDS OF THE DAY.
teach.b: Second, the first words of the day. In Sahih al-Bukhari, a companion reports that when the Prophet ﷺ went to bed he would say, in God's name I die and I live.

And when he woke he would say, in paraphrase: praise be to God, who gave us life after He had caused us to die, and to Him is the return. These words are kept as a morning remembrance, a dhikr, said on waking.
Third, to Him is the return. Waking isn't treated as proof that the end has been dodged. The same breath that gives thanks for this morning remembers a final return still ahead.
Gratitude and honesty sit in one sentence.
Jews have a short morning prayer, Modeh Ani, said on waking, thanking God for returning the soul with compassion. Two traditions, each in its own words, meet the morning as something given back.
For anyone, whatever they believe, the practice underneath is simple: notice that you woke up, and let the first words be thanks.

how: Muslims say a short remembrance on waking, praising God who gave life after sleep, as reported of the Prophet in Sahih al-Bukhari; Jews say Modeh Ani on waking, giving thanks for the returned soul.

o: waking each morning as a small return, met with thanks
getting back to work after a long rest or holiday
waking from a dream and finding it wasn't real

games.q: what's inside the morning words — tap the pairs.
p: souls taken in sleep, sent back
praise be to God who gave us life
thanks and honesty in one line

s: the Qur'an compares sleep to death
God takes souls at death, and in sleep, and sends some back until an appointed time.
the morning words treat waking as proof that death is avoided
they end: and to Him is the return.
the Prophet's bedtime words were, in God's name I die and I live
that's what the companion reports in Sahih al-Bukhari.

games.q: the Prophet ﷺ wakes up. what are his first words, as the companion reports them?
o: a list of the day's tasks.
praise be to God, who gave us life after He caused us to die.
a request for a longer life.
games.why: he praised God who gave life after sleep, and added: and to Him is the return.

practice: Close your eyes as if the day were over, let the body grow heavy, and rest for a few breaths, letting the day go.
Now slowly open them as if waking, notice the light, the room, the fact of being here again, and let one word of thanks rise, in whatever words are yours.
If you're Muslim, the Prophet's morning words may already be on your lips; if you pray in another way, your own morning prayer belongs here.

wordCard.voice: Awake again. Waking as a small return, met with thanks, as in the Prophet's morning words: praise be to God, who gave us life after He caused us to die. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: praise be to God. the words that open the Prophet's morning remembrance on waking.

carryVoice: Your line: to Him is the return. Each morning can open with thanks. That's day eight hundred fifteen.
